content.title: UConn vs. Michigan starting lineups: Yaxel Lendeborg, Solo Ball status
content.text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - MARCH 22: Tarris Reed Jr. #5 of the UConn Huskies celebrates with Alex Karaban #11 against the UCLA Bruins during the second round of the 2026 NCAA Men's Basketball Tournament.Mitchell Leff/Getty ImagesCollege basketball fans enjoyed arguably the most dynamic freshman class in recent memory this season, headlined by future NBA lottery picks A.J. Dybantsa, Cameron Boozer, Darryn Peterson and Caleb Wilson.As the calendar flips to April, however, these freshman phenoms have made way for a pair of ultra-experienced lineups to duke it out in the NCAA Tournament championship game Monday evening, as Michigan and UConn men's basketball meet. Indianapolis, IN 4/4/2026Erick W. Rasco/Sports Illustrated via Getty ImaLed by 23-year-old Yaxel Lendeborg and his fittingly frail left ankle, the Wolverines start four upperclassmen. The lone outlier, power forward Morez Johnson, offsets his sophomore status with an imposing 6-foot-9, 250-pound frame and a dominant low-post skillset. Meanwhile, UConn combines a similar reliance on veteran players with coach Dan Hurley's almost unmatched commitment to retention. Hurley has alloted 52.2% of UConn's minutes this season to returning players, including former national champions Alex Karaban and Solo Ball, a figure that ranks 19th nationally and trails only Purdue among high-major teams in the NCAA Tournament this season.Here's a player-by-player breakdown of how this experience manifests in each team's starting lineup. Article continues below this adUConnAlex Karaban (150 games played) — Alex Karaban's college basketball career will end with 151 games under his belt Monday evening as he looks to secure another national championship. That mark leaves him with the most games played in UConn history, along with a whole host of program records, but 28 games short of Jordan Bohannan's Division I record.Make CT Insider a preferred source on Google to see more of our journalism when you search.Add Preferred SourceThe Massachusetts native has been a nearly unprecedented contributor to winning basketball during his four-year stint in Storrs. Karaban has started in 19 NCAA Tournament wins as a Husky, which ties Bobby Hurley (19) and trails only Christian Laettner (21), and with a victory Monday, he would become the first non-UCLA player to win three national championships.Article continues below this adTarris Reed Jr. (135 games played) — Reed's long college basketball career began on the other side of Monday's national championship matchup, spending his first two seasons in maize and blue with Michigan. He's shown tremendous improvement to become the NCAA Tournament's most dominant interior player, struggling mightily with turnovers, foul trouble and motor during his freshman and sophomore years. Entering the transfer portal after the departure of Juwan Howard, Reed was lured to UConn ahead of the 2024-25 season, splitting time with Samson Johnson at the center position. Reed has flourished with an unquestioned grip on the starting job this year, averaging a 21-point double-double throughout UConn's NCAA Tournament run. INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - APRIL 04: Tarris Reed Jr. #5 of the Connecticut Huskies controls the ball in the second half against the Illinois Fighting Illini in the Final Four of the 2026 NCAA Men's Basketball Tournament at Lucas Oil Stadium.Brett Wilhelm/NCAA Photos via Getty ImagesSolo Ball (112 games played) — Ball is the other holdover from UConn's 2024 national title squad, although he played a comparatively minor role that season and earned just one garbage-time minute in the 75-60 championship game victory over Purdue alongside Jayden Ross and Andrew Hurley.Article continues below this adHe took a tremendous leap forward the following season, knocking down 99 3-pointers at an elite 41% clip and emerging as the Huskies' co-leading scorer. Ball has struggled with his perimeter shooting as a junior while battling a season-long wrist injury, but he stepped up with a crucial 10-point contribution in the second half of Saturday's Final Four matchup, helping UConn survive a late rally from Illinois.Silas Demary Jr. (108 games played) — The lone newly arriving transfer in UConn's starting lineup, Demary played the first 70 games of his college career at Georgia, picking up some post-season experience with a run to the NIT Semifinals as a freshman. Hurley made a relatively rare dip into the transfer portal for an upgrade at point guard, and Demary has certainly provided that during his debut season in Storrs, pairing the Big East's second-best assist rate with a much-needed defensive presence on the perimeter.Demary missed the first game of his college basketball career last month, sidelined from UConn's first-round NCAA Tournament matchup against Furman with an ankle sprain. The junior guard returned two days later against UCLA, but he has continued to battle pain and mobility issues throughout UConn's March Madness run. INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - APRIL 04: Keaton Wagler #23 of the Illinois Fighting Illini is defended by Silas Demary Jr. #2 of the UConn Huskies in the Final Four of the 2026 NCAA Men's Basketball Tournament at Lucas Oil Stadium.Michael Reaves/Getty ImagesBraylon Mullins (32 games played) — Mullins provides an infusion of youth and perimeter shooting into UConn's starting lineup, arriving in Storrs this summer as the premier 3-point specialist of the 2025 high school class. He's shown fortitude beyond his years in March Madness, however, hitting a pair of ultra-clutch daggers to help UConn reach Monday's title game.Article continues below this adThe Indiana native delivered the defining moment of his short college career last weekend against Duke in the Elite Eight, capping off a chaotic late-game sequence with a 35-foot heave to give UConn a 73-72 lead with 0.4 seconds remaining. In the Huskies' next game against Illinois, Mullins stepped up with a massive 3-pointer to give his squad a seven-point edge inside the final minute. MichiganAday Mara (99 games played) — The Spanish native began racking up high-level experience well before his college career began, debuting with the Basket Zaragoza first team in Liga ACB at just 16 years old. Mara arrived stateside in 2023 and played two seasons at UCLA before joining Michigan ahead of the 2025-26 campaign.Yaxel Lendeborg (109 games played*) — Lendeborg earns an asterisk due to his junior college career, playing 78 games at Arizona Western before making the jump to Division I. He spent the 2024 and 2025 seasons, blossoming into one of the nation's premier transfer portal prospects and a likely NBA Draft pick, only improving his stock with a tremendous year under Dusty May.Article continues below this adElliot Cadeau (111 games played) — Cadeau has authored quite the redemption story this season, committing to North Carolina as a highly-touted prospect in 2023 but ultimately electing to enter the transfer portal after two seasons amid highly-scrutinized struggles with 3-point shooters. The New Jersey native has shot nearly 38% from long range on high volume this season while posting one of the nation's best assist rates. INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - APRIL 04: Elliot Cadeau #3 of the Michigan Wolverines reacts after making a three-point basket during the second half of a NCAA Men's Basketball Tournament Final Four game against the Arizona Wildcats at Lucas Oil Stadium.Aaron J. Thornton/Getty ImagesNimari Burnett (147 games played) — Burnett is one of the final remaining beneficiaries of the extra COVID-19 season, beginning his career at Texas Tech in 2021 alongside Mac McClung, Terrence Shannon and future teammate Vladistav Goldin. After another stop at Alabama, Burnett has spent the last three seasons in Ann Arbor, developing into an elite 3-point threat. Article continues below this adMorez Johnson (79 games played) — Johnson is the least experienced player in Michigan's starting lineup, but he joined the Wolverines this offseason well-versed in the demands of Big Ten basketball. Starting eight straight conference games for Illinois last year before a late-season injury, Johnson has continued to develop under May, leading the conference with a 69.9% true shooting percentage.
